planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun; this species is dioecious, so a female tree is needed for berries and a male tree nearby improves pollination. Check local regulations before planting, as it is listed as an invasive noxious weed in Florida, Hawaii, and other frost-free regions.

directions: This fast-growing evergreen tree, native to Brazil, Paraguay, and Argentina, produces the small, bright red-pink drupes sold commercially as pink peppercorns, though botanically unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Harvest ripe berry clusters in late fall to winter once fully colored, then dry them whole for use as a mild, sweet-peppery spice or steep the dried berries in vinegar or brine. The tree is dioecious, so only female trees bear the ornamental red fruit clusters, and a nearby male is required for pollination. It tolerates poor soil, salt, and drought once established, but note that it is cashew-family (Anacardiaceae) and can trigger contact reactions in people sensitive to poison ivy or cashews, and is aggressively invasive in Florida and other subtropical regions where its cultivation is now restricted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in coastal hammock conditions with excellent drainage; this slow-growing species tolerates salt spray and drought once established but resents wet feet.

directions: Native to the Florida Keys, the Caribbean, and the Bahamas, this slow-growing evergreen shrub yields an aromatic cinnamon- and pepper-scented inner bark that was historically dried and used as a cinnamon substitute and pungent seasoning, and is still an ingredient in some Caribbean bay-rum style preparations. The glossy leathery leaves also release a peppery cinnamon scent when crushed and can be used sparingly as a seasoning. Grow in full sun to light shade in sharply drained, sandy or limestone soil; established plants are highly drought- and salt-tolerant coastal hammock natives. Clusters of small dark purple-red flowers give way to bright red pea-sized berries that ripen over winter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with shelter from strong wind and afternoon sun; this Patagonian rainforest species prefers cooler, wetter conditions than most spice trees.

directions: Native to the temperate rainforests of Chile and Argentina, this evergreen tree is named for the English navigator Captain William Winter, whose crew used its pungent, cinnamon-and-pepper-flavored bark as an antiscorbutic and spice in the 1570s. The aromatic bark, stripped in strips from branches, was historically dried and used as a pepper substitute, and is still occasionally used this way by foragers today. Unlike most tropical spice trees, it prefers cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil and part shade, tolerating more cold than true cinnamon or nutmeg but disliking hot, dry summers. Clusters of small ivory-white, jasmine-scented flowers appear in spring on mature specimens, followed by small blue-black berries.
sources: Pacific Bulb Society / specialty nursery references

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in sun to part shade; seeds are recalcitrant and best sown fresh in fall for spring germination rather than dried and stored.

directions: Native to the coastal forests and canyons of California and southern Oregon, this aromatic evergreen tree produces leathery leaves that are used fresh or dried as a bay leaf substitute in cooking, though its flavor and essential oil content are considerably more intense than Mediterranean bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) and a single leaf usually suffices per dish. Harvest individual leaves as needed year-round; crushing fresh leaves releases a pungent camphor-like aroma that has earned the tree the nickname "headache tree" among some foragers sensitive to its volatile oils. It tolerates a wide range of soils, from streamside to dry slopes, and can be kept pruned as a large shrub or hedge for easier leaf harvest rather than allowed to reach its full forest stature.

planting.note: Grow outdoors only in frost-free zones in rich, well-drained soil; elsewhere keep as a container plant moved indoors for winter, as with other Cinnamomum species.

directions: Endemic to the mountain forests of Taiwan, this cinnamon relative is prized because its leaves, rather than its bark, are the primary source of a high-cinnamaldehyde essential oil, making it possible to harvest cinnamon flavoring by repeated leaf pruning instead of destructively stripping bark. Individual wild trees vary widely in the dominant aromatic compound they produce (cinnamaldehyde, cinnamyl acetate, or camphor chemotypes), so named or clonal selections from cinnamaldehyde-type trees are preferred for culinary use. Grow in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; harvest and dry mature leaves for tea or as a ground cinnamon substitute, and prune to encourage flushes of new aromatic growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this species is classified as Endangered in the wild due to overharvesting of its bark, so only source nursery-propagated stock.

directions: Native to woodlands of southern and eastern Africa, this evergreen tree bears leaves and bark with a sharp, peppery bite, used fresh or dried as a chili-pepper-like seasoning as well as in traditional medicine, which has driven heavy wild harvesting and left the species classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Garden specimens should be grown from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected material, and only leaves (not bark) should be harvested from cultivated trees to keep the tree healthy, since debarking easily kills it. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; the tree is moderately drought-tolerant once established and produces small greenish flowers followed by purple-black fruits.
